utterances.text: Here we go. For the benefit of the Court, I will just read the exhibit numbers in a list format. P614, P621, D561, D554, D557, D552, D550, P606, and D543. And, again, these documents show the locations of the Ministry of Interior special police between the 4th and 9th of August, 1995, and then including the order on the 10th of August for the special police to go to Sector North, to Petrova Gora. That particular -- that particular order of August 10th was D557. We've also discussed the issue of abbreviations, Your Honour. Mr. Russo and I will sit down with those two exhibits, D267 and D268 and we will get that information to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, you had answered some questions previously regarding your knowledge or assumptions regarding the Ministry of Interior special police. Were you aware that the -- between August 4th and August 9th, the Ministry of Interior special police came down August 4th from the Velebit mountain through Gracac, Mazin, Donji Lapac, and ended up in Kulen-Vakuf Bosnia on the 8th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it was one of the axes of advance. I did not know it was the special police, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me, would you not, Mr. Berikoff, that if, in fact, the documents that I had just read off, the exhibit numbers both from the Prosecution and the Defence, show that between the 4th and 9th of August of 1995 the special police of the military police -- of the Ministry of Interior were not in the area of Knin, Drnis, Civljane, Kistanje, Cetina and Vrlika, you would have no facts upon which to base otherwise.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no other facts to base that on, and I would have to agree with what's on the documents, if that's what the documents say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please pull up 65 ter 2061. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a 11-page document which is a report of the military police units during Operation Storm dated August 13th of 1995. Mr. Berikoff, in the third paragraph there is an formation of the military police called the AT formation or anti-terrorist formation. Were you aware of that formation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that formation -- if it is the same as anti-sabotage or terrorist unit, yes, I was, because it was the same group -- or a group of people wearing the same type of patch I believe when President Tudjman came into the town of Knin, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did those people wear?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms and it had the crest with lightening bolts on it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, with AT formation of the military police do you know whether or not those formations were also called special police?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This particular report 13 August 1995, which is 65 ter 2061, discusses the various members recruited from the military police, the traffic police that were involved in Operation Storm. Were you at all familiar with these formations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to make one thing perfectly clear and we may have made this clear before, but I just want for the purposes of the record to make sure that it's clear. The military police that were -- that Major Juric commanded, it's true, is it not, that Major Juric, based on what you have learned today, had nothing to do with the Ministry of Interior special police.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot verify that. However, based on the information you said, I -- if they're accurate, that's true, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, again, if you refer to what the witness learned today, this assumes that he was in a position to draw any conclusions from what he has seen, and sometimes people learn things not as they were taught. I'm not saying that we're teaching the witness anything here. But the witness is limited to what he saw on paper today. Whether he learned that it's true what was on paper, whether he learned that the paperwork does not match with his own recollection, whether -- that's totally unclear. So, therefore, I would invite you to refrain from unspecified reference to what the witness learned today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I would like you to -- can you tell me without having known -- without having reviewed the documents today, irrespective of those documents, do you know whether Major Juric was the head of the special police of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I felt that he was a member and head of the military police/special police. The reason I say that is on numerous occasions that I had myself or myself with other people had run into Major Juric, he had the authority over the -- definitely over the military police throughout the sector at check-points that we got stopped at, it was Major Juric's name that was recognised beyond anybody else's, and when we first met Major Juric at the Ministry of Defence or in the police station it was Major Juric who seemed to command all of the control even when a lieutenant-colonel came into the room, it was the -- it was the major that was, in fact, giving the orders to the lieutenant-colonel, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please pull up D268. Page 2. Actually, we can start on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins had this document tendered into evidence and asked you some questions about it. This was an order from Major-General Lausic describing what Major Juric's tasks were, and if you look on the second page of this document, would you agree that at least as per this document, D268, there is nothing in this document that shows major Lausic, at least on paper, has any type of control over the Ministry of Interior special police?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the document, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to move 65 ter 2061 into evidence. I'd like to move that document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D737 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: By the way, I have 45 minutes, Your Honour, not an hour. Sean and I discussed this over the break, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this happens with the text authorities, you usually say you made a mistake. Now you are bound. I think we all accept the authority of our registrar for the time keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, just as an officer of the Court I wanted to make the Court aware I had less time than I had previously. Could we please call up P747.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before getting into P747, Mr. Berikoff, I enumerated a list of areas in which you thought you had seen the special police during the course of Operation Storm and shortly afterwards from the 4th and 9th of August. One area which I neglected to include was the area, the village of Strmica. I did not add that to the list of Knin, Drnis and other places. Would you agree with me that with respect to the village of Strmica the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Interior special police, at least according to the reports that I enumerated, was not in Strmica?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Back to P747. This was a list that you had compiled?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it was a day-by-day brief summary of places you had gone to. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now on the 8th of August, in 1 e you discuss HV troops or Croatian special police likely responsible for destruction in Knin. Now, based upon P614, which showed that -- which I had gone over with you earlier, that the special police, at that point in time, were located in Kulen Vakuf in Bosnia, the notation of Croatian special police being likely responsible is mistaken. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I received today, it's possible, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You also mention for example on August 11th the village of Civljane on page 2 of this document, which is 1 h. If we could go to page 2, please. Thank you. Again, on August 11th, you note you witnessed HV troops, including the special police, going into numerous residences. Again, going back to P641 by August 11th the special police were in Sector North, at least according to the documents that you were presented with earlier today. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I put in this document was based on the information I had and the assumptions I had at that time, sir, of people wearing grey coveralls and those wearing camouflage. However, based on the documents you showed me today, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you earlier referred to P614 which is among the documents you referred to at the beginning of the session after the break. Now we have 641. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It should be 614, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 614. And think you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see the transcript, but thank you. It's 614. If I said 641, I was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the 26th of November document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Similarly on August 11th, you note going into Donji Lapac, again, this is in P741, 1 i, when you go back to P614, Donji Lapac, the -- according to that document, the Croatian special police were already out of Donji Lapac as of August 8th, correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And, once again, my assumption was for the same reason, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And at least with respect to P614, any ID of Ministry of Interior special police, would you agree with me in areas identified as Cetina or Strmica or Kistanje is mistaken?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't say it's mistaken, sir. It was my assumption at the time based on the information I had. On the information I received today from you, according to the documents they were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, again, other than noting that they were in grey coveralls there's nothing specific about these people that would identify them as members of the Ministry of Interior special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to any of these people?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir. Other than Major Ivan Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go, please, to -- one of your statements, D284, page 22. The date of this statement, by the way, is May 26th and 27th of 1997, and we had Captain Hill here who testified earlier in this case, and he talked about this particular incident that I'm going to refer to between lines 18 and 36. One thing I'd like to ask you is, you state in the -- line 20 at the end of line 20: "We were forced out of our vehicle at gunpoint by a number of intoxicated Croat soldiers." Can you describe for me what do you mean by that? Can you describe for me how you knew they were intoxicated and what do you mean by intoxicated?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could smell alcohol on their breath. They were acting erratically, they were yelling and screaming at us, and mainly you could smell a vast amount of alcohol on their breath, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go to P748 for a moment, please. Page 9 of 17. If we could to the section of 9 August 1995. And about a third of the way down there's a sentence that begins at the far right-hand side. And I'll read this. "We went travelling in a 'restricted area' today just to see how far we could push the envelope. Very, very tense. I'm getting tired of being constantly afraid. We were stopped at an HV check-point near the KenBat headquarters today when one of the HV soldiers spotted the rifle that Geoff was carrying." Meaning Geoff Hill, correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "He went ballistic and forced us out of our vehicle at gunpoint. We were made to lay face down on the ground and wait. They took Captain Hill's weapon from him because it was a Serb AK-47, one that had been collected from a Serb soldier who was killed the first day of the offensive, pure stupidity on Jeff's part, and a HV soldier who actually came from Canada and could speak perfect English saved the day." Now, this from your daily journal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was made contemporaneous with roughly that day of August 9th, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And there's not one mention in this August 9, 1995 entry of someone being -- or anyone being intoxicated that confronted you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, to the best of my recollection, there was a strong stench of alcohol, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So two years later in 1997 you included the fact that you were stopped by a bunch of intoxicated Croatian soldiers while on August 9th of 1995, you simply say they were stopped at an HV check-point in a restricted area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The recollection of the alcohol was done or was recalled a lot earlier. It was two years later when I was spoken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You further say in this same paragraph in P748: "He," meaning the HV soldier who was from Canada, "and the Croat escort took us to meet the CO of KenBat. What a useless piece of trash." Are you referring to the CO of KenBat there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why was he a useless piece of trash?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall my opinion of why. He seemed -- at the time he seemed more interested in himself and didn't really care what was happening elsewhere and that is my opinion of him at that time, sir. I don't recall the whole incident of speaking with the CO of KenBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Three lines down from that you say: "We ran into Major Ivan Juric again. He asked us a few questions and was wondering why we were in a restricted area. We gave him some story which I'm sure he did not believe for a minute. He invited Geoff and I into a HV/HVO compound for a bite to eat." Now I noticed, Mr. Berikoff, that in several portions of your statements you use HV/HVO. Why do you use the term HVO? First of all, what is HVO?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO the Bosnian side of the Croatian military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And was there any identifying mark that would note these soldiers as HVO?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not, and that's why I put it down either/or, sir, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So HV/HVO was something that you just put down because you weren't sure?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. ... Yes, may I remind you of the pauses. At the same time, you mentioned KenBat several times. Now we know that sometimes CanBat is C-a-n-B-a-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and sometimes it is K-e-n-B-a-t. What did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this instances, Your Honour it's Kenya.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kenya, okay, then it is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: K-e-n, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I should have made that clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let go back to D284, same page, number 22. Now in May of 1997 as you described this incident at lines 23, you had talked about being forced out at gunpoint for a reason that was quite stupid on the part of Captain Geoff Hill. You also note on line 27 that not just Captain Hill but Corporal Tremblay decided to carry an AK because of the folding stock, rifle stock. So there were actually two Serb weapons in the vehicle. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were, there were Captain Hill and Corporal Tremblay who was Captain Hill's driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now were Captain Hill or Corporal Tremblay reprimanded ed for this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- I'm not sure about Corporal Tremblay. I do know for a fact that Captain Hill was reprimanded, because when we returned back to the UN compound I reported the incident to General Forand and General Forand, he also got quite upset about the incident and called Captain Hill in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of reprimand Captain Hill received?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to P729, please, and when we get there we can go just to the cover sheet at first. I don't think this is the document. Did I say 729?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The document I'm referring to, unless I wrote it down wrong and I'm sorry, is the daily journal -- yes, 729, Sean. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is P729.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you referring to the daily journal of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 30 July to 20 August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 July, yes, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, D729; my mistake. Thank you, counsel. Thank you, Mr. Registrar; my mistake. And that's page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, before we go to page 5 of this document, this is a daily journal that you compiled. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it an excerpt of the previous daily journal that I referred to, P748?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir. As I indicated at the beginning of my testimony, the journal was an ongoing project as I changed it from handwritten notes into electronic format.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we go to page 5 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And we, again, referenced the check-point incident of August -- 9 August. And in the middle of the paragraph -- or about a third of the way down in that entry, there's a sentence that begins with: "Went," w-e-n-t.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Went travelling again today in a restricted area. Very, very tense. I'm getting tired of being constantly being afraid. For example, today we got stopped at a Croat check-point near the Kenyan Battalion headquarters." And, again, the issue of the Serb AK that Captain Hill was carrying is referenced. There is no indication in this entry of you being accosted by intoxicated Croatian soldiers, is there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And this was on August 24th of 1996. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, that is not when the journal was done was August 1996. The journal was done ongoing as soon as I went to Sarajevo, if you recall from my answer the other day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do. What was the purpose of signing it on August 24th, 1996?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose that I signed was it was a document that I turned into the investigator during an interview, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 7 of this document toward the bottom, you have a notation here, it's the 12th of August, about the last quarter of the page, there's a sentence that -- on the right that begins: "We were spotted ..." And it says: "We were spotted by a number of HV special police (death squad) who surrounded us and placed us under arrest, supposedly for being in a restricted area." What is the HV special police death squad?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, from rumours or raw information that I had heard while I was there, people wearing the grey coveralls were also in many instances referred to as death squad. Some of that information came from the refugees in the camp. That's what they called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You have no evidence, factual evidence, to show that there were anything resembling a death squad in this area, do you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, was it your impression that -- or did you gain the impression during the course of your time that there were certain squads that went house to house?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was certain squads. But numerous soldiers and civilian police did go from house to house, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time, did you report your knowledge and information that you gained to your -- you did report your knowledge or information that you gained to your superiors. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following every -- every trip that I took throughout the sector, when I returned back to the compound, I gave verbal reports to General Forand and the operations staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And was that Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first couple of days it would have been Colonel Leslie. Later on it would have been the Jordanian Chief of Staff who I don't recall what his name is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now General Leslie, testified earlier that he left on the 7th or 8th of August of 1995. Does that square with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it was shortly after the offensive that he left, so, therefore, yes, it would have probably been the Jordanian Chief of Staff, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to pull up D329, just the transcript, please. Mr. Berikoff, earlier in this case during General Forand's testimony this document and transcript was introduced into evidence. It was an interview done in July of 2003 of General Forand and General Leslie regarding Operation Storm and its aftermath. Now, you had earlier testified that you had changed your opinion on the nature of the artillery attack on Knin, and I wanted to ask you a question about casualties during that time-frame. You've given us some estimate of -- or not some estimate, but you have given us some observations of a number of people that were dead that you had seen during the 4th and 5th of August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of that transcript, the third -- fourth paragraph, and I'll represent to you that L means Leslie, in answer to a question about shelling stated that the shelling, at the bottom, "it killed a lot of civilians and we'll never know the exact number but estimates range from 10 to 25.000 dead." Now, as intelligence and information officer for Sector South, you did not give that estimate range to General Leslie, did you no?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir, because I did not see anywhere near that amount. It was in the double or triple digits at the very most, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the number of 10 to 25.000 is flat wrong?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it is flat wrong based on the information I had at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now page 3 of this particular document in the middle, there's a comment by the reporter in the transcript that says: "General Leslie says that he saw Croatian police afterwards going house to house and killing anyone they found." And then the quotation is attributed to him: "There were a variety of organisations that then swept into the former Serbian Krajina. There were special police teams wearing their very distinctive blue uniforms who were engaged in hunting and killing in the mountains of Serbian civilians and I saw dozens and dozens of farm houses and even villages burning many, many days, in some cases, months after the initial assault had taken place." Now, I wanted to ask you a question about the special police teams wearing their very distinctive blue uniforms. Did you as the intelligence and information officer provide that information to General Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not because the only time I saw blue uniforms was when I was in fact in Bosnia when the Serbs were wearing blue uniforms. I did not see any blue uniforms in Croatia. They were the grey coveralls that I had seen in Croatia, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, were you aware at any time of any forces engaging in what Leslie, General Leslie called hunting and killing in the mountains of Serbian civilians?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, sir. I am aware of the destruction of homes in the area, but not of hunting and killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you know as a military intelligence information officer what kind of movements the ARSK had during the 5th and 6th of August in the area of Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, in the area of Donji Lapac, no, I don't, sir. It was later on that I learned and followed the route that they had withdrawn from the area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that before your arrival in Donji Lapac, I believe it was the 11th and 12th of August of 1995, that UNMO sitreps designated that there was looting going on by the army of BH coming across the border into Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the UNMO report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have access to UNMO reports at all, sitreps?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only access I had to UNMO reports were what was given to us in the morning prayers and it was a verbal report, not written. I did not see the UNMO reports. They would have gone through the operations, through a different chain of command to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please pull up P114. If we could go to page -- on the right-hand corner 9592, on the right-hand upper corner of this sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Toward the middle of this UNMO sitrep on this page there's a notation at 10 -- at 10 12.30 Bravo, meaning the 10th of August at 12.30 correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "At Donji Lapac UNMO patrol observed soldiers wearing BiH insignia helping refugees from Bihac with trucks to collect cows and other household items left behind by the Krajina Serbs." Now, you said you were not -- you did not observe that when you were there, on the 11th and 12th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you -- and I already talked to you about the fact that the Ministry of Interior special police were already out of Donji Lapac before the 10th of August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the document you showed me, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the ARSK, as they were going through Donji Lapac, was harassing the UN forces in the area and were demanding fuel before they left Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the harassing by the ARSK, that was ongoing when I first got there right until we left. As far as asking for fuel, I cannot respond to what they asked for up in the Donji Lapac area. I've already indicated the fuel issue in the Strmica area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we go to P111, please. If we could go to 9575 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Toward the middle of that document there's a discussion that around -- that on the 6th of August, ARSK trucks carrying 100 persons arrived at B platoon 5th, is that company?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir, 5th company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In Donji Lapac area and starting harassing and asking for fuel and rations. After negotiations with them, they left the area. Now, you were not in Donji Lapac until the 11th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the shelling that had gone on in Donji Lapac both before it was taken and after the Croatian special police entered Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. As I indicated earlier, I am aware of heavier combat activities up in that area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, if you could please tell us the nature and extent of the briefing that you got when you got to Zagreb before you became intelligence and information in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I virtually -- I was just given a general sitrep of the situation in the whole area of the former Yugoslavia and in particular in Sector South, saying that the situation was very tense, there was a likelihood of a possible HV offensive to retake the Krajina if negotiations that were being held were not successful. I was not given a detailed briefing to the extent of what forces were in the area, where they were located, or the identification of those forces, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would that be for both sides. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was for both sides, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And stated in one of your statements that on the 27th or 28th of July several local UN personnel did not show up for work and they were leaving the area.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you come to a conclusion as to why that was happening?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In the sense that there was also mobilisation of ARSK forces and it was my conclusion that a possible offensive by the HV was near at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that mobilisation I believe you had stated was broadcast on Radio Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the broadcast?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear it myself. I had heard from various sources including our operations staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can you please pull up P112. If we could go to 9581.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a sitrep, Mr. Berikoff, from the 8th of August of 1995, and on this page, at the bottom of the page, JorBat was on the border there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the border area near Donji Lapac, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Their headquarters was just north of the town of Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And this particular sitrep reports that on the 8th of August artillery shelling was reported in the general area at Boricevac from the BH side, correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So at least on the 8th of August, according to this sitrep, Donji Lapac was still in play in terms of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. And I indicated that previously as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you were kind enough to draw our attention to the corrected time given to you by -- you are now well -- you're over one hour and a half. Can you please try to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could have one moment, and I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One other question, Your Honour, and I will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, in the area of Boricevac were you aware of a very large weapons storage facility that was in that location?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Could you assist me in one of the documents, I think it was 614, refers to Otrovica. Could you assist me to find this on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the place, Your Honour? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Otrovica, I think it was. Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of Otravic, perhaps, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says Ostrovica. It was -- you referred to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, 26. On 31, it's on 26 as well. That is in Bosnia near Kulen Vakuf, Your Honour. That's across the border into Bosnia, where the special police ended their operation in Kulen Vakuf, at the edge of Kulen Vakuf. So Ostrovica is a village right next to Kulen Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Yes, may I then ask you in relation to the same page 31 of P614 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think it was, it is a draft translation on the second line, the semi-last word is their, t-h-e-i-r, which I would be inclined to read as there, t-h-e-r-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would agree, Your Honour, the second-last line where it says "engaged there," it should be t-h-e-r-e. The second their on the second-last line should be their own units. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree and we will see to it -- actually, this is a P document if I'm not mistaken. P614.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We can have that corrected. We'll work with the Prosecution to get that fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because one of the questions that came into my mind, and you might want pay further attention to it in the future, is special police forces that had been engaged there, what that exactly meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Being engaged there, whether -- how many there were and how limited that is -- or what limitations are included in that that had been engaged there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would estimate approximately 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will make my best attempt to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I'd like to take you back to a few areas covered during your cross-examination. Let me first ask Mr. President, I know on several occasions I will be referring to the transcript of the last two days. My particular transcript begins from 1 on every day, and I know that there was some issue about that with previous witnesses. I don't know if the Court's begins at a different number, but I can give it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can tell you very quickly. The 1st of September transcripts starts at page 7588, whereas the transcript of yesterday, the 2nd of September, starts at page 7702. So it takes some calculations, but I take it that you have access to e-court as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I just don't have the same page beginnings as you do and there's sometimes a bit of a miss. I have done the calculations although I think mine were off by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's ever any problem with the Word Wheel and search facilities, if you give a key word, then we will be able to find it rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Referring to transcript page - and the page starting from 1, it would be page 83 from lines 3 to 6, and I believe in Your Honours' transcript that would be page 7670 or 7671, depending where you begin. Mr. Kehoe asked you about the departure of civilians from Knin prior to Operation Storm and I believe Mr. Kuzmanovic just touched on it. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether you observed any RSK military or police involvement in the departure of those civilians?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the actual departure of the civilians, no, I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I noticed your qualification of the term actual departure. Does that mean that in some other fashion you saw their involvement?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Referring to page -- transcript 88, page 1 to 7, for Your Honours that would be transcript page 7675, 1 to 7, Mr. Kehoe asked you about whether the HV used the right type of ammunition for the destruction of buildings and facilities in Knin, and you indicated that they did. First let me ask you, approximately how many military buildings and facilities did the HV actually destroy in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that, sir, because I don't know how many military installations there were in Knin, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I'm just a little bit -- I apologise. I am a little bit confused on the pagination. I think the official transcript, Mr. Russo, 7675 covers the evacuation issue and this ammunition issue, I'm not sure I'm following the transcript exactly. My apologies. I certainly didn't mean to interrupt, but I think I have the official transcript and my pagination appears to be a tad different.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In any case, it should be approximately four to five pages beyond the departure issue. That is probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you give precise words. For example, you earlier used departure. Now departure appears not on my WordWheel there. So if you would give one word which is exact, then with WordWheel it is so easy to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I beg to differ. I'm not that quick. I'm a bit of a dinosaur. I'm still back on the old hard copy, so to the extent that we get some assistance on the hard copy, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I will try to assist both parties, Your Honour. With respect to departure issue the word to look for is evacuation. With respect to the questioning I'm now asking, the Court can look for destruction, buildings, or facilities and should find the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will say just for the record that the departure issue is the one that is on 7675. So if we can start from that premise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's line 5, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Russo, I'm just trying to stay with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So, Mr. Berikoff, first of all, let me get your definition of what it means for a building to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a building to be destroyed, it would mean that it's no longer inhabitable, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I understand your last answer was that you couldn't tell me how many military targets were destroyed. Can you give the Court an approximation of how many buildings in Knin were completely destroyed under your definition of that term?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under my definition of that term, I would say approximately 100 homes were destroyed during the offensive, and then following the offensive, looting, et cetera, and further destruction continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And taking homes out of that calculation, and speaking only about buildings or facilities and assuming these were not places where people are living, how many of those kinds of buildings or facilities did you see destroyed under your definition of that term?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give an accurate number. However, the -- the factory was hit, the POL portion was hit, the rail head was hit. There were also indications of shell impacts in and near the Ministry of Defence. The barracks at the northern end of town was also hit, the area of the police station, so I would consider these all military-type targets, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand that. I think you may be misunderstanding my question. You have named the factory, the POL station, the railway, the Ministry of Defence building, the barracks and the -- and the area around the police station. What I'm trying to determine is of those, how many were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give an accurate figure on that one, sir. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Regarding the weaponry that was used against Knin, I believe you've already testified and certainly it is in your statements that MBRL rockets were fired into Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you think that MBRL rockets are appropriate weapons to use against military targets in civilian-populated areas?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The multiple-barrel rocket launcher is an area weapon and a commander would definitely have to take into consideration the collateral damage that this has caused. I believe I explained there to Mr. Kehoe as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand your answer that a reasonable commander would have to take into consideration the damage that that would cause. Is that a particular concern where, as you call them, area weapons are used?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And from your perspective, are -- would the use of airburst ammunition be considered an area weapon?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Kehoe also asked you whether it would be reasonable for a military commander to fire artillery at the tanks which you saw driving through Knin on the morning of 5 August. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And let me just ask to you briefly to explain to the Court your understanding of how artillery should be used to hit a target that is moving through an urban area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends how the -- how the withdrawing force is leaving an urban area. If they are going in massive built-up areas the commander should consider the likelihood of collateral damage that it would cause, and if possible, it is better to use more of a weapon system that would be able to bring fire immediately upon the withdrawing force. However, as Mr. Kehoe indicated the other day, the -- the withdrawing force going through an area, yes, you would try to also eliminate that force, if possible, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't want to expand the scope of my question. Let's just take the example of -- you saw several tanks, if I'm not mistaken, several tanks making their way through Knin on the morning of 5th August, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court from your perspective what would be the appropriate way for a commander to engage those tanks with artillery?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- in -- now, this is just my opinion, but in my opinion the commander could wait until the tanks have gone out of the city on the outskirts and then engage them. However, it's up to the commander, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if the commander chose to engage them while they were driving through the city, would a reasonable commander expect that the likelihood of collateral damage would be higher than if he waited for those tanks to leave the city?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the whole concept of mobile targets is that targets are mobile, obviously, so if a tank is moving -- let me ask you this: How far can an ARSK tank move?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends what type of tank it is, sir. Some can go as high as 50 miles an hour, depending on the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, the model that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you'd take a breath now and then, the interpreters can do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court or give the Court some idea of how fast the kinds of ARSK tanks that you saw moving through Knin on the morning of the 5th can move.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The type of tanks that we saw moving through Knin were the older T-54, 55 tank and the old SU type tank and they are much slower than the newer model, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea how much slower?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: About half the speed or less, sir. They're also moving through a town of -- with streets, et cetera, and turns where they would have to slow down, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, do you know from which direction or directions the HV advanced toward Knin on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a couple of directions that they came. They came from the -- from the east and I -- and, as far as I am aware, they also came from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you know how far the HV advanced toward Knin from the east, by the end of 4 August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of 4 August, I believe they were within ten to 15 kilometres inside the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is that ten to 15 kilometres away from Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's ten to 15 kilometres from the border of the Krajina, coming either from the east or from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit D728.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And while that is being pulled up, Mr. Berikoff, can you tell me how far away Knin was from the confrontation line on the 4th of August, in the eastern direction?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could go it page 11 of D728.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, this is the -- if you'll recall the collection of maps that you generally agreed with and was admitted during Mr. Kehoe's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could, Mr. Registrar, please zoom in on the light blue area, immediately to the left of where it says "OG North," roughly the middle of the page. Further over to the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, the exhibit indicates that this light blue area immediately to the left of the letters OG North indicates that the HV, on the 4th of August, achieved some distance just within -- just beyond the confrontation line towards Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the map, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, did you agree with that map?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes, I did and I would say, yes, they came over the border about that far, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And looking at the map, I understand there's not a scale on the map, but judging the distance from Knin to that line, how many kilometres are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably ten to 15 kilometres from the eastern portion of the border, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how long would it take an artillery projectile fired from ten kilometres to reach Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the weapon system, sir, not very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give us an area of not very long?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I'm not artillery person.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Seconds?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be within seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Less than a minute?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than a minute, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. And in less than a minute would you agree that the tank could move from one position to another relatively -- even ten metres, 20 metres?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. And assuming that tanks are moving through Knin on the 5th of August, would a reasonable commander believe that firing artillery at those tanks from a distance of approximately ten kilometres away was going to be very effective?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends if the artillery was already targeted on a certain location that the tanks would be passing, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge, I would object on the scope because the -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I was listening to the French translation, which is a bit behind, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Much more interesting than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your words would be translated as well. Let me just read. Yes. You would object because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We are talking about a reasonable commander and what a reasonable commander knows and does at the time he fires in on a particular area. And that I think is the objection to the scope of this question. Because the question that counsel is asking is asking questions about what a reasonable commander would do which I trust. What this commander knew at the time i.e., General Gotovina or if it was a brigade commander doing the firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I think the objection to the extent that it is an objection that's clear that what was reasonable or not depends, often, on what the person acting knows or doesn't know. Sometimes it may include as well what he should have known. Would you please keep this in mind when continuing your line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. Mr. Kehoe had asked the same question with respect to a reasonable commander. I understand the qualifications to be the same and I do agree that it's what a reasonable commander would know at the time and what he should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So, Mr. Berikoff, in asking these questions please bear that in mind. Now, again, I'll restate the question. Assuming that there were tanks as you say moving through Knin on the 5th of August, would a reasonable commander believe that firing artillery at them from a distance of ten kilometres away is likely to be very effective?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not be very effective unless as I indicated earlier he had a pre-set target that he was firing upon and waited for those tanks to cross there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit D299.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, this was a document shown to you by Ms. Higgins and if you'll recall -- let's just wait till the English translation comes up. This is a document in which General Cermak is requesting the assistance of General Forand and his resources to remove damaged vehicles from the town of Knin. Now, did you hear from anyone in the HQ compound or anyone in the UN possibly assisting with this that anybody had to remove either a damaged or a destroyed tank from Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you personally observe a damaged or a destroyed tank in Knin after the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in attempting to destroy tanks that are moving through a city, would a reasonable commander have to consider the amount of collateral damage likely to occur from that attempt?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reasonable commander would definitely have to consider that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Based on what you personally observed, would you consider the amount of collateral damage to the residential areas of Knin to be extensive?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extensive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now at -- Mr. Kehoe also read you an intercept by General Mrksic on the 4th of August suggesting that ARSK forces had withdrawn from their positions for the defence of Knin. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me refer to your third statement which is tab 3 in your binder. It's Exhibit D84, at page 12, lines 1 through 13. For the court officer, this appears in the B/C/S at page 9, lines 7 through 23. Now, in that passage, Mr. Berikoff, you state your opinion that the stories being put out by the Krajina media on 4 August about the ARSK fighting and maintaining high spirits was all a deception because the ARSK had left the area and the town of Knin itself was extremely lightly defended. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And let me ask you: Did you see any evidence that -- personally observe any evidence that the ARSK forces actually made a defensive stand at or outside of Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally see them make the defensive. However, I did know where their defensive deployment area was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you know where that defensive deployment area was located on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the assumption that it was the same area where I had seen the positions prior to the offensive itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court where that was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the outskirts of Knin on the way to Otric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And was that area a civilian-populated area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was an open area on the outskirts of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kehoe also asked you whether the war lords that you referenced in your statement were wearing camouflage uniforms and other military paraphernalia and accoutrements, and I believe you agreed that they were. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: First of all let me ask you, please, to define for the Court what is it that you mean when you say the word war lord?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment of a warlord is like a gang leader. It will be a group of locals that get together and respond to the command and orders of an individual who they feel has authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you ever meet any individual that you would consider to be a warlord?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not meet any individual specifically. However, there were groups that appeared to be like a gang that definitely would not have responded to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are these the people that Mr. Kehoe asked you about and who you said were wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they are part of the group that Mr. Kehoe asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to any members of these groups?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically in the Cetina area when we were detained and taken to Vrlika police station, we were surrounded by such a group, and the one gentleman in particular got in the vehicle and escorted us to the Vrlika police station, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did that individual or any of the troops that you attribute to being part of a warlord's gang, did any of them ever tell you that they worked for a warlord or for anyone other than the Croatian military?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. It was just my assumption based on the type of uniform they were wearing, the disorganisation that existed and just the very -- various attitude that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to be clear about this. The only distinction you're drawing between what you call HV/HVO soldiers and the people in the service of these warlords is their uniforms and their attitude?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The uniforms, their attitude, their demeanour towards everybody basically, and -- yes, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did their demeanor include being drunk?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On numerous occasions there was alcohol involved, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to show you if I could, please, Exhibit P423. Looking at the people riding on that tank, Mr. Berikoff, how would you compare them to the people that you say you saw around the sector being in the service of warlords?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is similar to some of the people that I would say belonged to a group of warlords. However, they did not have in many instances those type of weapons systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't think you indicated earlier that the weapons systems were a basis that you used to distinguish between warlords and non-warlords. Focussing strictly on the uniforms that these people --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Object to commentary by counsel. If counsel wants to ask a question, that's fine, but I object to commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your objection is to be taken seriously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I was just trying to focus the witness on the fact that my question was not relating not to the weaponry but to the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you did more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Focussing Mr. Berikoff, just on the uniforms that these individuals in the photograph are wearing, how would you compare them with these warlords that you saw in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite similar, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you receive any information or intelligence from anyone to indicate that there were, in fact, warlords in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Right from -- right from 1991 when I worked on the Yugoslav crisis cell and onwards we were aware of groups of warlords as well as their local group of I guess soldiers, you can call them, and onwards. When I got to Knin I was also -- so I was aware in general that there were in fact groups of -- I would -- I don't know how to exactly describe them but that there were warlords with troops loyal to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that those warlords were not within the control of the HV?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Where did that understanding come from?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just from my understanding of a warlord and the group of troops they have loyal to them throughout -- throughout anywhere, Somalia, anywhere they are loyal to the warlord themself and not the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I would like to be very specific about the situation in Sector South immediately following Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand counsel doesn't like the answer but the question was just asked. He is asking the same question in a different fashion because didn't like the answer that the witness just gave. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I haven't asked my question yet so I'm not asking the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, whether Mr. Russo likes the answer or not, perhaps we'll -- he will never tell us, I don't know. He had not put the question yet. Mr. Russo, would you please focus on questions rather than on introductions to questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Court any particular location that is either a town or a particular area that you believe was controlled by a warlord immediately following Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In particular, I would say the town of Oklaj had a group of these type of people where they wore Rambo type shorts, cross-bandoliers bandannas on their head and had an attitude very unmilitary-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Other than Oklaj can you give the Court any other location that you believe was controlled by a warlord?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area around Cetina, I believe, was. Also areas around Razvode and the Macure area, I have also seen them up there. Other than that, I don't recall other specific names at this time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that we're at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even at half the hour you indicated, Mr. Russo. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I would estimate another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is more than you indicated before. I suggest that you try to conclude in the next six to seven minutes. Then we will have a break until 1.00 and then after the break there will be an opportunity for further questions from the Bench and perhaps from the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, you've just given us the areas of Cetina, Razvode and Macure. On the 12th of August, I believe you indicated that you were arrested by Croatian forces when you were watching the destruction IN Cetina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And weren't you taken to a police station after that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. However, we were taken to the police station by the Rambo type soldiers without -- they had the cross-bandoliers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you think that the Vrlika police station was under the control of a warlord?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe they were, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were the individuals in the grey coveralls also in Cetina when you were watching the destruction?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were at the check-point when we attempted to get into the Cetina area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you also see the individuals in grey coveralls in the area of Macure?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you ever see the people you identify as these warlords fighting with or against HV troops or individuals in grey coveralls?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, on the 9th of August, Mr. Kehoe and as well Mr. Kuzmanovic asked you about the incident where you were stopped at a check-point outside Bribirski Mostine by a drunken soldier. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I believe in your statements you refer to that person as sometimes a Croatian soldier but then you also use the term paramilitary organisation. Is that the same thing that you refer to as being one of these warlords?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a combination of both. They had HV soldiers as well as these -- I guess, paramilitary-type forces, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand. I'm trying to find out if you're equating paramilitary organisations with warlords?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitary, yes, I am, based with the warlord and gang-type style of grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer to mean that HV soldiers were also working with these groups that check-point?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my understanding that's how it was, yes, now, but that's all my understand was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you were pulled out of your vehicle by drunken soldiers, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I think your diary that you just indicated during Mr. Kuzmanovic' cross-examination, it was a HV liaison officer that came to the rescue?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did the HV liaison officer have to fight with or otherwise threaten the drunken soldiers in order to get you released?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did get in a heated discussion. However, at the end of the day the liaison officer was able to negotiate and take us to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did the liaison officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just for clarification, there is only one reference in one statement and it refers to one intoxicated soldier. I thought that was -- not intoxicated soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Berikoff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the question has to be put again. Did you understand the question to refer to the event where you said you have seen one indicated soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I don't think there is any need to further repeat the question. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, did the HV liaison officer have to brandish a weapon at the drunken soldier in order to get you released?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him brandishing a weapon. I know there was a heated discussion. Whether he -- I can't recall the weapon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you were questioned by Mr. Kehoe concerning whether or not you thought that the Croatian forces had the ability to stop these warlord-type people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you've made a number of indications in your statements and also during your testimony here about the level of authority that you perceived Major Juric to have. From your perspective do you think that Major Juric had the ability to stop these warlords, if he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it would have been extremely difficult for Major Juric to have stopped these -- these warlords and their -- their troops or their followers. They were very unruly, and they had a different type of demeanour about them. So it would have been extremely difficult for him as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: From your perspective, were these warlord-type people more equipped weaponry wise than the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some instances, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated during, I believe, Ms. Higgins examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could I ask one question. "More equipped weaponry wise than the Croatian forces," what did they have more, are you talking about quantity or about quality, and if you are talking about quality, could you tell us what they have, the Croatian forces did not have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about both, Your Honour, both in quantity but at times also quality where they would have various types of western type equipment, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is still a bit too vague to me. Is it same type of weaponry but more modern and from western fabrication or would it be other types of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More modern and from western fabrication, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've stolen one and a half minutes from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicated, Mr. Berikoff, during Ms. Higgins' examination that the letter that you had from Cermak was a joke, and I think there was a suggestion that Mr. Cermak's authority was totally ineffective outside of Knin. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken to the Vrlika station, what was it that got you released from the Vrlika station on the 12th of August? We're talking after the Cetina incident.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
